name: Digital Logic & Computer Organization
desc: Boolean algebra, combinational & sequential logic, instructions, addressing, pipelining, memory, I/O, RAID

topics.name: Boolean Functions & K-Map Simplification
notes: n variables → **2ⁿ minterms** (and 2ⁿ maxterms). 2 vars → 4, 3 vars → 8, 4 vars → 16.
**Minterm** = AND term containing every variable once (true for exactly one input row). **Maxterm** = OR term (false for exactly one row).
**SOP** = sum of minterms Σm(...). **POS** = product of maxterms ΠM(...). Σm and ΠM of a function use complementary index lists.
K-map cells are labelled in **Gray code** (00, 01, 11, 10) so adjacent cells differ in one bit.
K-map groups must be powers of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8…), rectangular, and may wrap around edges. Bigger groups = simpler terms.
**Quine–McCluskey (tabulation) method**: function is given as a list of minterm numbers (decimal integers); group by number of 1s, combine terms differing in one bit → prime implicants.
**Absorption**: X + XY = X, X(X + Y) = X. So X + XY' + XY'Z = X (needs zero gates).
**De Morgan**: (A·B)' = A' + B', (A + B)' = A'·B'.
NAND and NOR are **universal gates** — any function can be built from only NAND or only NOR.
A **don't-care (X)** can be treated as 1 or 0, whichever gives a bigger group.

topics.name: Combinational Logic: Adders, Encoders, Decoders, MUX
notes: **Combinational circuit**: output depends only on present inputs (no memory). Examples: adder, subtractor, MUX, DEMUX, encoder, decoder, comparator.
**Half adder**: Sum = A ⊕ B, Carry = A·B. **Full adder**: Sum = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin, Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B). A full adder = 2 half adders + 1 OR gate.
**Half subtractor**: Diff = A ⊕ B, Borrow = A'B. **Full subtractor**: Diff = A ⊕ B ⊕ Bin.
**Decoder**: n inputs → 2ⁿ outputs (one output active per binary code). A 1-of-32 decoder can be built from four 3-to-8 decoders (plus a 2-to-4 to enable them).
**Encoder**: 2ⁿ inputs → n outputs (reverse of decoder). **Priority encoder** encodes the highest-priority active input.
**MUX** (data selector): 2ⁿ data inputs, n select lines, 1 output. **DEMUX**: 1 input → one of 2ⁿ outputs.
**Parity** is generated/checked with **XOR/XNOR** gates (XOR of all bits = 1 when an odd number of 1s).
**Magnitude comparator** outputs A>B, A=B, A<B — exactly one of them is 1 at a time.
To choose 1 of N items you need ⌈log₂N⌉ bits/switches. 8 doors → 3 switches.

topics.name: Sequential Logic: Latches, Flip-Flops & Counters
notes: **Sequential circuit**: output depends on present inputs **and** past state (has memory). Built from latches/flip-flops.
**SR latch** (active-HIGH): S=1,R=0 → SET (Q=1); S=0,R=1 → RESET (Q=0); S=0,R=0 → **no change (hold)**; S=1,R=1 → invalid.
**JK flip-flop**: J=K=0 hold, J=1,K=0 set, J=0,K=1 reset, **J=K=1 toggle**. Toggling halves the frequency (20 kHz clock → 10 kHz output).
**D flip-flop**: Q follows D when enabled/clocked (Q⁺ = D). **T flip-flop**: T=1 toggles.
**Master–slave**: master is enabled when the clock is **HIGH**, slave when the clock is LOW. Fixes the race-around problem.
**Ones catching**: a master–slave JK can wrongly "catch" a glitch (unwanted 1) on J or K while the clock is HIGH.
**Race-around**: in a level-triggered JK with J=K=1, the output toggles many times while the clock is HIGH. Fixed by master–slave or edge triggering.
A **MOD-N counter** needs **⌈log₂N⌉ flip-flops**. MOD-32 → 5, divide-by-128 → 7. n flip-flops divide the frequency by up to 2ⁿ.
**Asynchronous (ripple) counter**: clock goes only to the first flip-flop, so delays add up. **Synchronous counter**: clock goes to **all stages at the same time** → no ripple delay.

topics.name: Data Representation & Number Codes
notes: **Signed n-bit ranges**: sign-magnitude and **1's complement → −(2ⁿ⁻¹−1) to +(2ⁿ⁻¹−1)** (two zeros). **2's complement → −2ⁿ⁻¹ to +(2ⁿ⁻¹−1)**. 8-bit: 1's = −127..127, 2's = −128..127.
**2's complement** = invert all bits + 1. −5 in 8 bits: 00000101 → 11111010 → **11111011 = FB₁₆**.
**Gray code** (reflected binary code): MSB is the same; each next Gray bit = XOR of adjacent binary bits. 101011 → 111110. Only one bit changes between successive values.
**Gray → binary**: binary bit = previous binary bit XOR current Gray bit.
**BCD** (8421): each decimal digit in 4 bits. 0001 0010 0110 = 126 = 1111110₂. Valid BCD digits are 0000–1001.
**Excess-3** = BCD + 3 (self-complementing code). Gray code and Excess-3 are **unweighted** codes.
**IEEE 754 single precision**: 1 sign + 8 exponent (bias 127) + 23 mantissa = 32 bits. Double: 1 + 11 (bias 1023) + 52 = 64 bits.
**Booth's algorithm** multiplies two signed binary numbers in 2's complement form.
**Overflow** in 2's complement addition happens when two numbers of the same sign give a result of the opposite sign.

topics.name: Basic Computer Organization & Control Unit
notes: **MAR** (Memory Address Register) holds the address being accessed; **MDR/DR** (Memory Data Register) holds the data being read or written. **PC** holds the address of the next instruction. **IR** holds the current instruction.
**Memory read**: CPU puts the address into MAR → data comes into MDR. **Memory write**: address into MAR (AR) **and** data into MDR (DR), then write.
The CPU supplies the location address and puts it on the **address bus**. Data moves over the **data bus**. (In this question bank the memory bus is equated with the data bus.)
**Instruction cycle** = full sequence the CPU performs per instruction: fetch → decode → (fetch operands) → execute → (interrupt check).
**Control memory** stores microinstructions (microprograms) and is usually a **ROM** inside the micro-programmed control unit.
**Hardwired control** = fast, built from gates (RISC). **Microprogrammed control** = flexible, microcode in control memory (CISC).
CPU modes: **Executive (supervisor) mode** is used while servicing interrupts / running the OS; **Task (user) mode** runs programs. Control memory addresses are divided into these 2 modes.
**SDRAM** = Synchronous Dynamic RAM. **DDR2** = Double Data Rate 2 (transfers data on both clock edges). **IRET** = Interrupt Return.

topics.name: Instructions, Types & Formats
notes: An instruction = **opcode** (operation) + **operand/address field(s)**. An instruction code must specify the operation and the **address of the operand**.
**Instruction types**: data transfer (MOV, LOAD, STORE), arithmetic/logical (ADD, AND), program control/branch (JMP, CALL, RET), I/O.
**Formats by number of addresses**: 3-address (ADD R1,A,B), 2-address (ADD R1,A), 1-address (accumulator: ADD A), 0-address (stack: ADD).
Fewer addresses → shorter instructions but more instructions per program.
**Zero-address instructions** use a **stack** (operands are on top of the stack): PUSH A, PUSH B, ADD.
**One-address** instructions use an implied **accumulator** (AC).
**RISC**: few simple fixed-length instructions, load/store, many registers, hardwired control, easy pipelining. **CISC**: many complex variable-length instructions, microprogrammed.

topics.name: Addressing Modes
notes: **Immediate**: operand is **in the instruction** itself (MOV A, #5). Fastest — no memory access for the data.
**Direct (absolute)**: address field = **effective address** of the operand in memory. Simplest mode that fetches the operand from memory (1 memory reference).
**Indirect**: address field points to a memory word that holds the **effective address** (2 memory references).
**Register**: operand is in a CPU register. It works like direct addressing, but the address field names a register.
**Register indirect**: register holds the effective address (e.g. MOV A, @R0).
**Displacement** (EA = A + (R)): very powerful mode — covers **relative** (R = PC), **base-register** and **indexed** addressing.
**Implied**: operand is implied by the opcode (e.g. CMA complements the accumulator; zero-address stack instructions).
**Auto-increment/decrement**: register indirect + automatic update of the register — good for arrays.

topics.name: Pipelining
notes: **Pipelining** overlaps execution of instructions in stages (e.g. IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB). It improves **throughput**, not the latency of one instruction.
Time for n instructions on a k-stage pipeline = **(k + n − 1) × cycle time**. Non-pipelined = n × k cycles.
**Speed-up** = n·k / (k + n − 1) → approaches **k** (the number of stages) for large n.
**Hazards**: **Structural** (resource conflict), **Data** (instruction needs a result not ready yet: RAW, WAR, WAW), **Control/branch** (branch target unknown).
Fixes: **forwarding/bypassing** and stalls (bubbles) for data hazards; **branch prediction**, delayed branch for control hazards; duplicating resources for structural hazards.
**RAW (read after write)** = true dependency — the most common data hazard.
Pipeline cycle time = slowest stage delay + latch/register delay.

topics.name: Memory Hierarchy & Cache Memory
notes: **Hierarchy** (fast/small/costly → slow/large/cheap): Registers → Cache (L1, L2, L3) → Main memory (RAM) → Secondary storage (SSD/HDD) → Tertiary (tape).
**Locality of reference** makes caches work: **temporal** (reuse soon) and **spatial** (nearby addresses soon).

**Cache mapping** decides where a block goes / how the cache is searched: **Direct** (block → exactly one line: line = block mod lines), **Associative** (any line), **Set-associative** (any line within one set).
**Hit ratio** h = hits / total accesses. **Avg access time** = h·Tc + (1 − h)·(Tc + Tm) (or h·Tc + (1−h)·Tm, depending on the model).
**Write-through**: write to cache and memory together. **Write-back**: write to memory only when the block is replaced (dirty bit).
Misses — the 3 Cs: **Compulsory** (first access), **Capacity** (cache too small), **Conflict** (mapping collision).
Replacement: **LRU**, FIFO, random (not needed for direct mapping).
Direct-mapped address = **Tag | Line (index) | Word (offset)**.

topics.name: Virtual Memory
notes: **Virtual memory** lets programs use an address space larger than physical memory by keeping parts on disk and loading them on demand.
Implemented by **paging** (fixed-size pages/frames) or **segmentation** (variable-size logical segments).
**MMU** translates virtual → physical addresses using the **page table**. The **TLB** is a small fast cache of recent translations.
**Page fault**: the page is not in memory → OS loads it from disk (swap).
Number of pages = virtual address space / page size. Offset bits = log₂(page size).
**Effective memory access time with TLB** = h(t + m) + (1−h)(t + 2m) for a single-level page table.
**Thrashing**: too many page faults → CPU busy swapping, little useful work.

topics.name: I/O Techniques, DMA & Interrupts
notes: **Three I/O techniques**: **Programmed I/O** (CPU busy-waits/polls), **Interrupt-driven I/O** (device interrupts the CPU when ready), **DMA** (controller moves blocks directly between device and memory).

**DMA**: the CPU only sets up the transfer (address, count, direction), then is free; the DMA controller takes over the system bus (**cycle stealing** or **burst mode**) and interrupts the CPU at the end.
**Priority interrupt** establishes a priority among sources to decide which request to serve first. Implemented by **polling** (software) or **daisy chaining** (hardware, serial priority).
**Daisy chaining**: devices are connected in series; the device nearest to the CPU has the highest priority.
**Vectored interrupt**: the device supplies the address (vector) of its service routine. **Non-maskable interrupt (NMI)** cannot be disabled.
On an interrupt: finish the current instruction → save PC & status → jump to the ISR → **IRET** restores the state.

**I/O interface** handles differences in speed, data format and signals between CPU and peripherals. **Memory-mapped I/O** uses the same address space as memory; **isolated I/O** uses separate IN/OUT instructions.

topics.name: RAID Architecture
notes: **RAID** = Redundant Array of Independent (Inexpensive) Disks — several disks act as one for performance and/or reliability.
**RAID 0**: striping, **no redundancy** — fastest, no fault tolerance.
**RAID 1**: mirroring — data duplicated on 2 disks; 50% capacity overhead.
**RAID 2**: bit-level striping with Hamming-code ECC (obsolete). **RAID 3**: byte-level striping + one dedicated parity disk.
**RAID 4**: block-level striping + one **dedicated** parity disk (the parity disk is a bottleneck).
**RAID 5**: block-level striping with **distributed** parity — survives 1 disk failure. Usable capacity = (n−1) disks.
**RAID 6**: like RAID 5 with **double distributed parity** — survives 2 disk failures. Usable = (n−2) disks.
**RAID 10 (1+0)**: a stripe of mirrors — fast and fault tolerant.

w: Only a ring counter would use 10.

questions.q: The maximum count of a 6-bit binary counter (starting at 0) is:
w: 64 is the number of states (0–63), not the maximum count.

questions.q: How many flip-flops are needed for a counter that divides the clock frequency by 64?
The reason behind that the delay problems faced in asynchronous counters is eliminated by Synchronous counters :
o: input clock pulses are applied only to the first and last stages
input clock pulses are applied only to the last stage
input clock pulses are not used to activate any of the counter stages
input clock pulses are applied simultaneously to each stage
w: Wrong — that's not how either works.
All flip-flops share one clock, so they change together — no ripple delay.
questions.h: Synchronous = common clock to ALL stages at once.

questions.q: In an asynchronous (ripple) counter, the clock pulse is applied to:
o: Only the first flip-flop; each later stage is clocked by the previous stage's output
questions.h: Ripple = clock only the first stage; delays add up.

questions.q: The main disadvantage of a ripple counter is:
o: Propagation delays accumulate, limiting the maximum speed
It needs a separate clock for each stage
w: Same number of flip-flops as synchronous.
Each stage waits for the previous one.
It can count up or down.
It uses only one clock input.

questions.q: A circuit whose output depends on present inputs AND past outputs is called:
How '-5' is represented in hex format in 2’s complement in 8-bits?
The 8-bit 2's complement representation of −1 in hexadecimal is:
The 8-bit 2's complement of −12 is:
The 1's complement of the 8-bit number 0101 1010 is:

A computer has a word length of 8 bits (including sign). It is required to determine the range of integers that can be stored in the computer. If 1’s complement is used to represent the numbers, then the range will be
w: 1's complement: −(2⁷−1) to +(2⁷−1); it has two zeros (+0 and −0).

questions.q: The range of an 8-bit 2's complement number is:
w: 2's complement has a single zero, so one extra negative value.

questions.q: The range of a 16-bit sign-magnitude integer is:
Which representation has two representations for zero?
Which of the following code is also known as rereflected code
w: Gray code is the "reflected binary code" — the list mirrors itself.

questions.q: Which property defines the Gray code?
o: Successive values differ in exactly one bit
It adds 3 to every BCD digit
w: This is why it is used in K-maps and rotary encoders.

questions.q: Choose the gray code form for the binary value 101011?
questions.h: Binary→Gray: copy MSB, then XOR each neighbouring pair.

questions.q: The Gray code of binary 1011 is:
The Gray code 1101 converts to binary as:
questions.h: Gray→Binary: each binary bit = previous binary bit ⊕ current Gray bit.

questions.q: Consider Binary coded decimal value 0001 0010 0110 . Convert the given value to binary form.
questions.h: BCD → read each nibble as a digit → decimal → binary.

questions.q: The BCD representation of decimal 59 is:
w: 1010 is not a valid BCD digit.
questions.h: BCD = one nibble per decimal digit.

questions.q: Which of these is an INVALID BCD code?
w: 1100 = 12; BCD digits only go up to 1001 (9).

questions.q: The Excess-3 code of decimal 4 is:
In IEEE 754 single precision format, the exponent field is:
Which algorithm is a multiplication algorithm which multiplies two signed binary numbers in 2’s complement notation
w: Booth's algorithm handles signed 2's-complement operands directly.
Only Booth's is designed for signed 2's complement.

questions.q: In Booth's algorithm, when the current bit pair (Qᵢ, Qᵢ₋₁) is (1, 0), the multiplicand is:
w: 10 = start of a run of 1s → subtract M.

questions.q: In Booth's algorithm, bit pairs 00 and 11 cause:
w: Inside a run of 0s or 1s nothing is added.
The loop runs for n bits.

questions.q: Overflow in 2's complement addition occurs when:
o: Two numbers of opposite signs are added
Two numbers of the same sign produce a result of the opposite sign
There is a carry out of the MSB
w: E.g. +100 + +100 in 8 bits gives a negative number.
A carry out alone is not overflow in 2's complement.

questions.q: In memory transfer location address is supplied by____ that puts this on address bus
w: The ALU does arithmetic, it does not drive addresses.
The CPU (via its MAR) supplies the address and places it on the address bus.
MAR is the register inside the CPU; the bank's answer is the CPU as a whole.
questions.h: CPU drives the address bus (from its MAR).
questions.f: Technically the address sits in the MAR, which is part of the CPU. The bank key is "CPU"; choose CPU if this exact question appears.

questions.q: Operation of memory transfer are
w: Memory transfers are reads (memory→CPU) and writes (CPU→memory).

questions.q: In memory, the read operation puts memory address on to a register known as
w: PC holds the next instruction's address, not every memory address.
The Memory Address Register holds the address to be read.

questions.q: Which operation puts memory address in memory address register and data in DR
w: In a read, data comes OUT of memory into DR afterwards; you don't put data in first.
For a write, the CPU loads the address into AR/MAR and the data to be stored into DR, then writes.
Only write loads data into DR beforehand.
questions.h: Write = address + data both loaded first.

questions.q: Which register holds the data that has just been read from memory or is about to be written?
w: The data register is the buffer between memory and CPU.

questions.q: The program counter (PC) holds:
o: The address of the next instruction to be fetched
w: PC is incremented after each fetch.

questions.q: The memory bus is also referred as______
w: The bank treats the memory bus as the data bus that carries data between CPU and memory.
questions.h: Memory bus ↔ data bus (per this question bank).
questions.f: Strictly, a memory bus has both address and data lines. This bank's key is "Data bus".

questions.q: Which bus is unidirectional (from CPU to memory/devices)?
questions.h: Address bus = one way. Data bus = two way.

questions.q: A CPU with a 16-bit address bus can directly address how much memory (byte-addressable)?
______is the sequence of operations performed by CPU in processing an instruction
w: The instruction cycle covers fetch, decode, execute (and interrupt check).

questions.q: The correct order of phases in a basic instruction cycle is:
w: Get the instruction, work out what it means, then do it.

questions.q: During the fetch cycle, which happens first?
o: Contents of PC are transferred to MAR
w: The address of the instruction must go out first.

questions.q: Control memory is part of ______ that has addressable storage registers and used as temporary storage for data
w: The bank expects ROM: control memory is a ROM holding microinstructions.
The bank expects the memory type, ROM.
questions.h: Control memory = ROM inside the control unit.
questions.f: The question wording is garbled. Control memory is typically a ROM inside the CPU's microprogrammed control unit. Pick ROM, as the bank does.

questions.q: Microprograms are usually stored in
w: Microcode is fixed, so it is kept in ROM (control memory).
Volatile, and microcode doesn't need to change.
Sequential access memory is too slow.

questions.q: A control unit that uses microinstructions stored in control memory is called:
w: Uses fixed gates, not stored microcode.
Control signals come from microinstructions in control memory.

questions.q: Compared with microprogrammed control, hardwired control is:
w: Gates are fast, but any change needs redesign.
questions.h: Hardwired = fast & rigid (RISC). Microprogrammed = slower & flexible (CISC).

questions.q: How many modes the address in control memory are divided into?
w: Two modes: executive mode and task mode.

questions.q: Mode of addresses in control memory are:
w: The two modes are executive and task.

questions.q: which of the following is interrupt mode
w: Interrupts are handled in executive (supervisor) mode.

questions.q: User application programs normally run in which mode?
w: Reserved for the OS and interrupt handling.
Normal programs run in task/user mode.

questions.q: IRET stand for
w: IRET returns from an interrupt service routine, restoring flags and PC.

questions.q: SDRAM stand for
w: SDRAM is synchronised with the system clock.

questions.q: DDR2 stands for
w: Transfers data on both rising and falling clock edges.
questions.h: DDR = Double Data Rate (both clock edges).

questions.q: DDR memory achieves higher bandwidth because it:
o: Transfers data on both the rising and falling edges of the clock
questions.h: Double Data Rate = 2 transfers per clock.

questions.q: DRAM needs periodic refreshing because:
o: Data is stored as charge on capacitors that leaks away
w: That is SRAM, which needs no refresh.
questions.h: DRAM = capacitor (leaks) → refresh. SRAM = flip-flop (no refresh).

questions.q: An instruction code must specify the address of the____
w: The opcode is the operation itself — it has no address.
The address field tells where the operand (data) is.

questions.q: The part of an instruction that specifies the operation to be performed is the:
w: Tells how to interpret the address.

questions.q: An opcode field of 7 bits can specify at most how many distinct operations?
A computer has 32 instructions and 8 registers. The minimum bits for the opcode is:
Zero-address instructions are used in which type of organisation?
w: Operands are implicitly on the top of the stack (e.g. ADD pops two, pushes the sum).

questions.q: One-address instructions use an implied register called the:
w: e.g. ADD X means AC ← AC + M[X].

questions.q: The instruction ADD R1, R2, R3 is an example of:
w: Destination plus two sources are listed.

questions.q: Which is a characteristic of RISC processors?
o: Simple fixed-length instructions and load/store architecture

questions.q: JMP, CALL and RET belong to which type of instruction?
w: They change the flow of execution.

questions.q: In which addressing the operand is actually present in instruction
w: The operand value is part of the instruction itself (e.g. #5).
The instruction holds the operand's address, not the operand.
The operand is in a register.

questions.q: In which addressing the simplest addressing mode where an operand is fetched from memory is_____
w: No memory fetch is needed — the operand is in the instruction.
The address field gives the effective address directly → one memory access.
Operand comes from a register, not memory.
questions.h: Direct = simplest mode that goes to memory for data.

questions.q: which addressing is a way of direct addressing
w: The operand is in the instruction.
It cannot be "a way of" itself.
Register addressing is like direct addressing, except the address field names a register instead of a memory location.
questions.h: Register addressing = direct addressing on registers.

questions.q: In which mode the main memory location holds the Effective Address of the operand
w: The operand is in the instruction.
The instruction holds the EA itself.
The operand is in a register.
The instruction points to a memory word whose content is the EA.

questions.q: Which addressing is an extremely influential way of addressing
w: EA = A + (R) — very powerful; covers relative, base-register and indexed modes.

questions.q: In displacement addressing, the effective address is computed as:
w: Address field plus the contents of a register.

questions.q: Relative addressing is a form of displacement addressing in which the register used is the:
w: EA = PC + offset — used for branches.

questions.q: Which addressing mode needs TWO memory accesses to get the operand (after the instruction fetch)?
w: One access to fetch the EA, a second to fetch the operand.

questions.q: The instruction `MOV A, @R0` (operand address is inside R0) uses:
w: That would use R0's value as the operand.
R0 holds the address of the operand.
No memory address is written in the instruction.

questions.q: Which addressing mode is most suitable for accessing array elements in a loop?
w: EA = base + index, and the index changes each iteration.

questions.q: The instruction CMA (complement accumulator) uses which addressing mode?
w: The operand (accumulator) is implied by the opcode.

questions.q: Which addressing mode is the fastest for getting the operand?
w: The operand comes with the instruction, so no extra access is needed.
Needs an address calculation plus a memory access.

questions.q: The main benefit of instruction pipelining is:
o: Reducing the execution time of each individual instruction
Removing the need for a cache
w: Latency per instruction does not drop (it may even rise slightly).
Several instructions are in different stages at once.

questions.q: A 5-stage pipeline with a 1 ns clock executes 100 instructions (no stalls). Total time is:
w: Off by one: it is k + n − 1.

questions.q: The ideal maximum speed-up of a k-stage pipeline is approximately:
w: For a very large number of instructions, n·k/(k+n−1) → k.

questions.q: A 4-stage pipeline runs 20 instructions. Speed-up over a non-pipelined machine with the same stage time is:
w: That is the ideal limit for infinite n.

questions.q: When an instruction needs the result of a previous instruction that is not yet available, it is a:
w: That is a hardware resource conflict.
A memory event, not a pipeline hazard class.

questions.q: Hazards caused by branch instructions are called:
w: The next instruction address is unknown until the branch is resolved.
That is a data hazard type.

questions.q: Two instructions need the same memory unit in the same clock cycle. This is a:
w: A resource conflict — fixed by duplicating resources (e.g. split I/D caches).

questions.q: Operand forwarding (bypassing) is used to reduce:
w: The result is passed straight from a later stage to the ALU input without waiting for write-back.

questions.q: Which data hazard is a true dependency?
w: The instruction really needs the value produced earlier.

questions.q: Branch prediction is a technique to reduce:
w: It guesses the branch outcome so the pipeline keeps fetching.

questions.q: The stages of a pipeline have delays 150, 120, 160 and 140 ps; latch delay is 10 ps. The pipeline clock period is:
On what method search in cache memory used by the system
w: The mapping function (direct/associative/set-associative) decides where to look in the cache.
That marks stale lines; it is not a search method.
questions.h: Where is the block? → Cache MAPPING.

questions.q: In direct-mapped cache, a memory block can be placed in:
w: Line = block number mod number of lines.

questions.q: In fully associative mapping, a block can be placed:
w: Most flexible; needs parallel tag comparison.

questions.q: A cache has 64 lines. Using direct mapping, main memory block 200 maps to line:
w: 200 ÷ 64 = 3 is the tag, not the line.

questions.q: A cache with 128 blocks is 4-way set associative. The number of sets is:
w: That is the ways (blocks per set).
That is the total number of lines.

questions.q: Which cache mapping technique needs no replacement algorithm?
w: Each block has only one possible line, so there is no choice to make.
questions.h: Direct mapping: no choice → no replacement policy.

questions.q: A program repeatedly accessing the same variable within a short time shows:
questions.h: Temporal = time (same item again). Spatial = space (neighbours).

questions.q: Accessing array elements a[0], a[1], a[2]… one after another shows:
w: Not the same element each time.

questions.q: Cache hit ratio is 0.9, cache access time is 10 ns, main memory access time is 100 ns. Average access time (hierarchical: on a miss you check cache then memory) is:
w: That is the miss time only.

questions.q: Cache hit ratio 0.8, cache 20 ns, memory 120 ns, simultaneous (parallel) access. Average access time is:
In the write-back policy, main memory is updated:
o: On every write to the cache
Only when a modified (dirty) block is replaced

questions.q: Which memory is the fastest in the memory hierarchy?
w: Inside the CPU, accessed in a single cycle.
Very fast, but registers are faster.

questions.q: As we move down the memory hierarchy (away from the CPU):
o: Capacity increases and access time increases
questions.h: Down the pyramid: bigger, slower, cheaper.

questions.q: A cache miss that occurs on the very first access to a block is called a:
w: The block has never been loaded before.
Caused by the cache being too small.

questions.q: In a direct-mapped cache, the memory address is divided into:
w: The line field picks the cache line, the tag confirms the block.

questions.q: Virtual memory allows:
o: Programs to run without any main memory
A program's address space to be larger than physical main memory
w: Main memory is still needed for the active parts.
questions.h: Virtual memory = illusion of a big memory.

questions.q: The hardware unit that translates virtual addresses to physical addresses is the:
w: Uses page tables / TLB to translate.

questions.q: The TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer) is:
o: A small fast cache of recent page-table entries
w: It avoids a page-table memory access on a hit.
It caches part of the page table.

questions.q: A virtual address is 32 bits and the page size is 4 KB. The number of virtual pages is:
w: That is the page size in bytes.
Offset = 12 bits (4 KB), so page-number bits = 32 − 12 = 20.
That is the number of bytes.

questions.q: When a referenced page is not present in main memory, it is called a:
w: The OS must bring the page from disk.
questions.h: Page not in RAM → page fault.

questions.q: With a TLB hit ratio of 80%, TLB access 20 ns and memory access 100 ns, the effective memory access time (single-level paging) is:
w: That is the hit time only.
That is the miss time only.

questions.q: . ________interrupt establishes a priority over the various sources to determine which request should be entertained first
w: A priority interrupt system decides which simultaneous request to serve first.
Polling is one software way to implement priority, not the general term.
A hardware way to implement priority, not the general term.
questions.h: Who goes first? → PRIORITY interrupt (done by polling or daisy chain).

questions.q: In daisy-chain priority, the device with the highest priority is:
o: The one electrically closest to the CPU
The one farthest from the CPU
The one with the largest buffer
w: The acknowledge signal reaches it first.

questions.q: Polling as a method of priority interrupt is implemented in:
o: Software — the CPU checks devices one by one in priority order
w: That is daisy chaining / parallel priority.

questions.q: In which I/O technique does the CPU keep checking the device status in a loop?
w: The device signals the CPU instead.
That is an addressing scheme, not a transfer technique.

questions.q: Direct Memory Access (DMA) is used to:
o: Let the CPU access cache faster
Transfer blocks of data between I/O and memory without the CPU moving each word
w: The DMA controller takes over the bus.

questions.q: In DMA, the CPU is involved:
o: Only at the start (set-up) and at the end (completion interrupt)
w: It must set up the transfer.
questions.h: DMA: CPU sets up, controller transfers, interrupt says done.

questions.q: In cycle-stealing DMA mode, the DMA controller:
o: Takes the bus for one cycle at a time, interleaving with the CPU
Holds the bus until the entire block is transferred
w: CPU slows slightly but keeps running.
questions.h: Cycle stealing = one word at a time. Burst = whole block.

questions.q: Which DMA controller registers are set up by the CPU before a transfer?
o: Address register and word-count register (plus control/direction)
w: They tell where and how much to transfer.

questions.q: Which interrupt cannot be disabled by software?
w: Used for critical events like power failure.
About how the ISR address is found, not masking.

questions.q: In a vectored interrupt:
o: The interrupting device supplies the address of its service routine
w: The CPU jumps directly to that vector.
questions.h: Vector = the device says where to go.

questions.q: When an interrupt occurs, the CPU first:
o: Completes the current instruction, then saves the PC and status
w: So it can return with IRET.

questions.q: I/O devices that share the same address space as memory and are accessed with normal load/store instructions use:
w: No special I/O instructions are needed.

questions.q: RAID stands for:
w: Multiple disks combined for speed and/or reliability.
questions.h: RAID = Redundant Array of Independent Disks.

questions.q: Which RAID level provides striping with NO redundancy?
w: Best performance but any single disk failure loses data.

questions.q: Which RAID level uses mirroring?
w: Each disk has an identical copy.

questions.q: Which RAID level uses block-level striping with parity distributed across all disks?
w: Byte-level with a dedicated parity disk.
Parity blocks rotate across disks, removing the parity-disk bottleneck.

questions.q: Which RAID level can survive the failure of any TWO disks?
w: Two independent parity blocks per stripe.

questions.q: The bottleneck of RAID 4 is:
o: The single dedicated parity disk, which every write must update
w: RAID 5 fixes this by distributing parity.

questions.q: In a RAID 5 array with 5 disks of 2 TB each, the usable capacity is:
w: One disk's worth goes to parity: (5−1) × 2 TB.

questions.q: In RAID 1 with two 4 TB disks, the usable capacity is:
w: The second disk is a full copy.

questions.q: RAID 10 (1+0) combines:
w: Stripe across mirrored pairs for speed + redundancy.

questions.q: Which RAID level uses Hamming code for error correction?
w: Bit-level striping with Hamming ECC disks.
